scenes.subtitle: A 60-second explainer
scenes.narration: Have you ever wondered what that little padlock by a web address actually means? Let us find out.

scenes.title: Life without HTTPS
scenes.narration: Plain HTTP sends everything as plain text. On an open network, anyone nearby could read your messages, or even change them while they travel.

scenes.title: The handshake
scenes.narration: HTTPS starts with a quick handshake. The browser and the server greet each other, the server proves its identity with a certificate, and they agree on secret keys known only to them.

scenes.label: of Chrome page loads are HTTPS
scenes.narration: Today, more than ninety five percent of page loads in Google Chrome happen over HTTPS, up from barely half just a decade ago.

scenes.title: Share of Chrome traffic
scenes.narration: On Chrome, encrypted traffic grew from around fifty percent in twenty fifteen to more than ninety five percent by the early twenty twenties.

scenes.title: Who vouches for a site
scenes.narration: Certificates come from certificate authorities, trusted organizations vetted by browser makers. When a certificate is wrong or expired, your browser stops you before any data is sent.

scenes.label: the port HTTPS always uses
scenes.narration: One number is worth remembering. HTTPS always connects on port four hundred and forty three, while plain HTTP uses port eighty.

scenes.subtitle: Your data will thank you
scenes.narration: So next time you log in, glance for the padlock and the letters H T T P S. That small check keeps your secrets yours.
